title: clocksync-induced-routing-jitter-llama-mistral-qwen
content:
Summary:

Informal investigation into how host/GPU clock skew and timestamp ordering anomalies correlate with MoE routing jitter and long-context KV-cache mis-evictions across Llama/Mistral/Qwen runs. We observed routing misorders (gating decisions that diverge across replicas) that coincide with sub-5ms timestamp drifts between nodes, causing increased tail latency and occasional token duplication in stitch traces.

Why this matters (high level):
- MoE routing decisions are time-sensitive in our pipeline: gating + prefetch windows assume consistent ordering across worker traces.
- Long-context KV cache eviction and prefix caching rely on consistent event timestamps to merge/evict correctly.
- Small clock skews change the ordering of request/response events in the global trace, which our aggregation layer treats as causality, leading to stale prefetch/incorrect fanout in some edge cases.

Observed symptoms (prod-ish repro runs):
- 95th/99th token-latency spikes during mixed-batch MoE workloads on clusters spanning two availability zones.
- Router-side traces show fanout counts oscillating by +-1 between otherwise-identical replicas for the same request id.
- KV cache eviction logs show short-lived cache misses immediately after a large low-rate burst (suspected misordered evict triggers).
- Small proportion (~0.4%) of requests see duplicated tokens in stitched response (post-merge).

Quick repro notes (how we reproduced in lab):
- Setup: 4-node cluster (A,B in AZ1; C,D in AZ2). Model variants: 13B MoE Llama-like, Mistral 7B mix, Qwen-14B.
- Time config: intentionally desynced NTPd on node C by +3ms, node D by -2ms.
- Tooling: trace-injector v0.3 to feed identical request batches to all nodes; logging level = debug on router, gating, kv-layer.
- Observed: routing gating timestamps on C/D shifted, gating thresholds for prefetch window moved relative to upstream token emission, causing C/D to prefetch one expert less/more.

Representative trace excerpt (simplified):
- req=abc123 node=A t=12:01:01.102 router:gate-eval fanout=2
- req=abc123 node=C t=12:01:01.099 router:gate-eval fanout=1  <-- earlier timestamp, gate took different branch
- req=abc123 node=A t=12:01:01.206 kv:prefetch schedule=enqueued exp=42
- req=abc123 node=C t=12:01:01.204 kv:prefetch canceled cause=merge-order-mismatch
- merge-layer: later merge found missing shard from node C -> triggers retry -> increases end-to-end latency

Microbenchmarks we ran: (profiling harness attached in linked PR)
- Kernel-level event sync: cudaEventElapsedTime shows consistent relative ordering when using local monotonic GPU clocks, but host-side timestamps (gettimeofday) differ across nodes by 1-8ms under default NTP config.
- Synthetic gating-only workload: with 10k requests, desync=5ms -> 0.9% fanout divergence; desync=0.5ms -> 0.03% divergence.
- KV eviction stress: contiguous long-context (>=32k tokens) with desync=3ms produced +12% cache churn vs baseline.

Root cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) Aggregation/merge layer uses wall-clock timestamps from hosts to establish causal order for cross-replica gating/kv ops. Small skews flip ordering.
2) Router/gating code assumes monotonicity of host timestamps for micro-windows (prefetch guard windows of 2-4ms).
3) CUDA event profiling differences mask actual compute ordering; our traces prefer host timestamps but kernel completion is gated by GPU stream events (misaligned semantics).

Immediate mitigations tried and effects:
- Enforced PTP sync on test cluster (PTPd locked): fanout divergence dropped to near-zero; latency tails reduced by ~9% in synthetic runs.
- Switch merge-layer to use per-request logical counters incremented by router (instead of host time) for ordering within a request scope: fixed divergence in lab but required touching many components.
- Add a small safety-buffer of 6ms to prefetch window (i.e., broaden gating decision window): reduced misfires but increased unnecessary prefetching ~2.2% which impacted bandwidth.

Longer-term solutions to evaluate:
- Move to logical clocks per-request (sequencer token) propagated from ingress; use this as canonical ordering for intra-request operations. Pros: independent of wall-clock; cons: requires protocol change + handling replays/fails gracefully.
- Prefer monotonic timestamps (clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW)) on host-to-host protocol; ensure trace aggregation normalizes by node-offset computed at connection start.
- Use GPU-side timestamps (cudaEvent record) for kernel completions and map to host timeline using a high-frequency sync handshake (every N seconds) to avoid drift effects.
- Fallback routing stability: if two replicas disagree on fanout, prefer the higher-fanout decision for safety (idempotent) or use a deterministic tie-breaker.

Open questions / unresolved:
- How often do these conditions appear in customer workloads vs internal synthetic bursts? Some of our customer traces show similar patterns but we need signal/labeling to be confident.
- Does model architecture matter beyond kernel latency (i.e., does Mistral's shorter layer time reduce exposure window)? Preliminary: models with shorter per-token compute are less sensitive because absolute ordering windows shrink.
- Are there corner cases where fanout divergence is actually beneficial (e.g., adaptive load shedding)? We saw none in tests; likely not.

Action plan (next 6 weeks):
- Short term (1 week): enable monotonic host timestamps in dev clusters and add note to tracing infra (ENG-1426).
- Mid term (2-3 weeks): prototype per-request logical sequence token in canary path for a single tenant and measure divergence/latency.
- Long term (6+ weeks): design GPU-host sync mapping layer; evaluate PTP vs logical clock approach, propose interface changes to merge-layer tracing API.

Notes / build commands / snippets:
- quick trace capture: ./scripts/capture-trace --nodes A,B,C,D --duration 120 --level debug > trace.log
- enable ptp (dev): sudo systemctl stop ntpd && sudo systemctl start ptpd && ptp4l -m -i eth0
- switch to monotonic in code: replace gettimeofday() usage in merge_layer with clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW, ...) and compute per-connection base_offset at handshake time.

References and context links:
- Related PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/3174 (tracing + logical-clock stub)
- Jira: JIRA-ENG-1426 (trace normalization for multi-az clusters)
- Confluence draft: confluence.redwood.internal/clock-sync-drift (notes, spreadsheets)

Appendix: quick checklist for oncall/ops when similar incident occurs:
- Check cluster clocks: sudo chronyc tracking / ptp4l status
- Collect router/gate logs for the request id; look for fanout inconsistency across nodes in 10-20ms range
- If incident is ongoing, temporarily enable safer one-sided routing (prefer max-fanout) to reduce retries
- File postmortem with traces attached and correlate with kube node time drift metrics

Thoughts: this feels like a low-frequency, high-impact bug class. Fixing at the trace/ordering layer (logical tokens + monotonic host timestamps) should eliminate root cause without massive perf cost; PTP is a useful operational patch but brittle for diverse customer infra.

TODOs:
- [ ] Add automated unit test that reorders host timestamps by +/-5ms and asserts merge-layer idempotency (Liang)
- [ ] Run a customer workload replay with per-request logical token canary (Marta)
- [ ] Prepare short-run PTP rollout guide for Dedicated customers (ops)

Tags for later search: clock skew, ordering, trace normalization, prefetch-window, merge-layer, MoE, kv-eviction

End of notes.
